notes: In Chicago shootings outside rise 1.140 (1.127 to 1.152) per 5 C and shootings classed inside rise 1.102 (1.074 to 1.129). The inside slope is smaller, as registered, with a margin of 0.006 below 1.00 (z about 2.4). New York's finding that inside shootings do not rise (1.009, 0.975 to 1.044) is not reproduced with the registered classes. The classes are flawed: 2,132 of the 5,746 incidents classed inside (37%) have descriptions that also match the outside pattern (porch or hallway 1,043; parking lot or garage 669; residence yard 240; hospital building or grounds 171), because the inside pattern was tested first. The error pulls the ratio toward 1.00, against the claim. Exploratory, deciding nothing: with ambiguous descriptions excluded the ratio is 0.918 (0.888 to 0.948) and the inside slope 1.046; homes only against street, alley and sidewalk give 0.932 (0.899 to 0.965) and 1.056. With the registered classes the ratio is 0.969 with year-by-month terms, 0.977 (0.931 to 1.026) in May to September, 0.953 in 2010 to 2017 and 0.979 (0.945 to 1.014) in 2018 to 2026. What transfers from New York is the direction: shootings inside rise less with heat than shootings outside. Whether the two cities differ in size is not shown; Chicago homes against New York inside differ by z = 1.9 on a classification chosen after the data. The undated counts quoted in the registration's already_seen came from a narrower preview query (gunshot_injury_i = 'YES' and two incident types) and are smaller than the counts the script fetched.
